To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

KIF1A is a rare cause of HSP with a very low prevalence of the AD- SPG30 subtype, that variants in KIF 1A are mostly located within the motor domain and that the clinical phenotype of KIF1A- related HSP is highly variable.
we have identified four new KIF1A variants in four HSP patients, two of whom carrying the same p.S69L variant previously reported in a single AD-SPG family.

we have found four novel variants in KIFIA gene, which is a gene involved in a subtype of hereditary Spastic Paraparesis, and that the variants we found fall in the same regions of previously reported variants.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of a rare form of hereditary spactic paraparesis due to variants in KIFIA.
the identification of the genetic causes of HSP and with a better understanding of the molecular basis of the disease.
the identification of the molecular mechanisms of a rare form of neurodegeneration, hereditary spastic ataxia type 1 (HSA1) caused by mutations in the KIF1A (kinesin family member 1A) gene.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
KIF1A is a rare cause of HSP, but that the KIF1A-associated HSP is not a rare disease.
KIF1A is a very rare cause of HSP.
KIF1A is not a frequent cause of HSP, but that it may contribute to the genetic heterogeneity of this disease, particularly in the AD-SPGS30 subtype.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
KIF1A is an important gene for HSP and the motor domain is the most frequently mutated domain.
KIF1A is a rare cause of HSP, but its identification in HSP patients should be considered, particularly in those with a positive family history.
the KIF1A is a gene with a very low frequency in HSP and a very wide clinical phenotype.
The main takeaway from our work is that
KIF1A is not only involved in recessive forms of SPG, but it can also be responsible for the AD-SP30 phenotype.
